title: What are the producer partitioning strategies (round-robin when no key, hash-of-key for ordering per key, custom `Partitioner`), and how does each affect ordering and load distribution?
shortTitle: Producer partitioning strategies (round-robin, hash-of-key, custom) and their effect on ordering and load
keyPoints: No key means the sticky (or round-robin) partitioner spreads records evenly for maximum throughput but provides no ordering.
A key triggers murmur2 hashing modulo partition count, so the same key always maps to the same partition for per-key ordering.
A custom Partitioner implements business logic such as routing premium accounts to dedicated partitions.
Ordering is only guaranteed within a single partition, never across partitions.
The sticky partitioner in modern Kafka fills one batch before switching partitions, improving batch efficiency.
Changing partition count rehashes keys and breaks key-to-partition mapping for in-flight data.
A custom partitioner must be tested and maintained as production code.

s1_definition.oneliner: No key means round-robin for even load but no ordering; a key means hash-of-key for per-key ordering; a custom partitioner lets business rules decide, trading off ordering and balance.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Sticky partitioner (no key)** -- the default when no key is provided; fills one partition batch, then switches to another, spreading records evenly for throughput but providing no ordering between related records.
- **Hash-of-key partitioner** -- when a key is present, computes `murmur2(key) % numPartitions` so the same key always maps to the same partition, giving per-key ordering.
- **Custom Partitioner** -- implements `org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.Partitioner` and overrides the `partition` method with business logic, such as routing by account tier.
- **Ordering guarantee** -- Kafka guarantees order only within a single partition; two records on different partitions have no ordering relationship.
- **Explicit partition** -- you can bypass the partitioner by passing a partition number directly in the `ProducerRecord`, used rarely and carefully.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India directing customers to teller windows. Round-robin with no key is like a greeter who sends the next customer to whichever window is free -- all windows stay busy but one customer's two visits might go to different windows. Hash-of-key is like saying every customer always goes to the window matching the last digit of their account -- one account's transactions are always handled in order. A custom partitioner is like a VIP rule: premium accounts always go to a dedicated express window.

sections.s6_takeaway:
There are three producer partitioning strategies, and each makes a different trade-off. When a record has no key, the sticky partitioner fills batches efficiently and spreads records evenly across partitions for maximum throughput, but provides no ordering between related records. When a record has a key, the default partitioner hashes it modulo the partition count so the same key always maps to the same partition, giving per-key ordering.

A custom partitioner lets business logic override the default. At National Bank of India, Pankaj implements Kafka's Partitioner interface to route premium corporate accounts to dedicated partitions so their settlement gets guaranteed consumer capacity. Audit events are keyless and round-robin for throughput, transfer events are keyed by account id for strict per-account ordering.

The critical constraint is that ordering is only ever within a partition, never across partitions. Changing the partition count rehashes keys and moves them to different partitions, breaking ordering across the boundary. A custom partitioner is powerful but becomes production code that must be tested and maintained.

Remember one sentence: partitioning is where you encode both your correctness requirement through ordering and your performance requirement through balance, so decide the ordering need first and pick the key that satisfies it.
